claim: CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans combine the CloudFront CDN with multiple AWS services and features into a monthly price with no overage charges. With a flat-rate plan you never face overage charges, even during traffic spikes or attacks.
question: Are there overage charges on a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan?

evidence.quote: CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans combine the CloudFront CDN with multiple AWS services and features into a monthly price with no overage charges.

With flat-rate plans, you pay one price that includes multiple AWS services like CloudFront, WAF, Route 53, S3, and CloudWatch Logs and never face overage charges, even during traffic spikes or attacks.

note: FAQ items 17 and 18. Flat-rate plans are newer than the 2022 exam guide; the dated change fact (d130) carries the date. Plan terms can change, hence volatile.

claim: Attack traffic never counts against a flat-rate plan's usage allowance. This includes both blocked DDoS attacks and requests blocked by AWS WAF.
question: Do DDoS attacks and WAF-blocked requests count against a CloudFront flat-rate plan's usage allowance?

values.display: never counts against your plan’s usage allowance

qualifiers.scope: CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans, usage allowance

evidence.quote: No, attack traffic never counts against your plan’s usage allowance.
This includes both blocked DDoS attacks and requests blocked by AWS WAF.

claim: Flat-rate plans suit you if you want combined monthly billing, simplified service configuration and built-in security features without worrying about overage charges. Pay-as-you-go suits you if you need complete control over individual service features, custom configurations, features not available in flat-rate plans, or expect large, predictable traffic spikes.
question: When does the CloudFront FAQ say to choose flat-rate plans and when to choose pay-as-you-go pricing?

values.display: complete control over individual service features

qualifiers.scope: CloudFront flat-rate plans compared with pay-as-you-go

evidence.quote: Flat-rate plans are ideal if you want combined monthly billing, simplified service configuration, and built-in security features without worrying about overage charges.

Pay-as-you-go pricing is a better choice if you need complete control over individual service features, custom configurations, access to features not available in flat-rate plans, or if you expect to handle large, predictable traffic spikes.

claim: When you invalidate objects individually, you can have invalidation requests for up to 3,000 objects per distribution in progress at one time. That can be one request for 3,000 objects, 3,000 requests for one object each, or any other combination that does not exceed 3,000 objects.
question: How many objects can be in progress in invalidation requests per distribution at one time when objects are invalidated individually, according to the CloudFront FAQ?

qualifiers.scope: per distribution, invalidation requests in progress at one time, objects invalidated individually
qualifiers.condition: the FAQ states this limit; the user guide quota page states a different invalidation quota (paths or tags per second)

evidence.quote: If you're invalidating objects individually, you can have invalidation requests for up to 3,000 objects per distribution in progress at one time.
This can be one invalidation request for up to 3,000 objects, up to 3,000 requests for one object each, or any other combination that doesn't exceed 3,000 objects.

note: FAQ item 42. CONFLICT TO WATCH: the user guide quota table (cloudfront-limits, 'Quotas on invalidations') gives 150 paths or tags per second and 1 wildcard invalidation per second, not an in-progress count. The FAQ is tier 2; the guide wins. The adjustable flag is false because the FAQ does not say the limit can be raised.

claim: When you use the * wildcard, you can have requests for up to 15 invalidation paths in progress at one time. This limit is independent of the limit on invalidating objects individually.
question: How many wildcard invalidation paths can be in progress at one time, according to the CloudFront FAQ?

values.display: independent of the limit on invalidating objects individually

qualifiers.scope: wildcard invalidation paths in progress at one time (per distribution)
qualifiers.condition: the FAQ states this limit; the user guide quota page states a different invalidation quota

evidence.quote: If you're using the * wildcard, you can have requests for up to 15 invalidation paths in progress at one time.

You can also have invalidation requests for up to 3,000 individual objects per distribution in progress at the same time; the limit on wildcard invalidation requests is independent of the limit on invalidating objects individually.

note: FAQ item 42. Same conflict as cloudfront-faq-invalidation-individual-objects-in-progress; the FAQ does not say the limit is per distribution for the wildcard sentence, so the scope is left as the FAQ gives it.

claim: You can remove a file from edge locations by deleting it from the origin; it is removed when the content reaches the expiration period in its HTTP header. To remove harmful material before that time, you can use the Invalidation API to remove the object from all CloudFront edge locations.
question: How do you remove an object from CloudFront edge locations before its expiration time?

qualifiers.condition: removal before the expiration time needs the Invalidation API

evidence.quote: You can simply delete the file from your origin and as content in the edge locations reaches the expiration period defined in each object’s HTTP header, it will be removed.

In the event that offensive or potentially harmful material needs to be removed before the specified expiration time, you can use the Invalidation API to remove the object from all Amazon CloudFront edge locations.

claim: If your files do not change often, set a long expiration period and use a versioning system to manage updates. If files will need to be removed from cache frequently, the FAQ recommends a versioning system and/or a short expiration period instead of invalidation.
question: What does the CloudFront FAQ recommend instead of frequent invalidation when files change often?

qualifiers.condition: files need to be removed from cache frequently

evidence.quote: If your files don’t change very often, it is best practice to set a long expiration period and implement a versioning system to manage updates to your files.

You should use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances; if you know beforehand that your files will need to be removed from cache frequently, it is recommended that you either implement a versioning system for your files and/or set a short expiration period.

question: Which HTTP request methods does CloudFront support?

enable caching for the responses to OPTIONS requests

You may enable caching for the responses to OPTIONS requests.

note: FAQ item 57. Compare the user guide page on cached HTTP methods (GET, HEAD, optionally OPTIONS).

claim: To deliver content over HTTPS using your own domain name and your own SSL certificate, you use one of the Custom SSL certificate support features of CloudFront.
question: How can you deliver content over HTTPS with your own domain name and your own SSL certificate on CloudFront?

values.display: your own domain name and your own SSL certificate

qualifiers.scope: CloudFront HTTPS delivery with a custom domain name

evidence.quote: If you want to deliver your content over HTTPS using your own domain name and your own SSL certificate, you can use one of our Custom SSL certificate support features.

claim: Field-Level Encryption lets you securely upload user-submitted data such as credit card numbers to your origin servers. CloudFront encrypts sensitive data in an HTTPS form with field-specific encryption keys that you supply, before a PUT or POST request is forwarded to your origin.
question: What is CloudFront Field-Level Encryption and what does it protect?

qualifiers.condition: applies to PUT/POST requests before they are forwarded to the origin

evidence.quote: Field-Level Encryption is a feature of CloudFront that allows you to securely upload user-submitted data such as credit card numbers to your origin servers.
Using this functionality, you can further encrypt sensitive data in an HTTPS form using field-specific encryption keys (which you supply) before a PUT/ POST request is forwarded to your origin.

claim: With field-level encryption, CloudFront edge locations encrypt the sensitive data, and from that point only applications that have the private keys can decrypt the sensitive fields. Even if an application service leaks cipher text, the data remains cryptographically protected.
question: Who can decrypt data that CloudFront field-level encryption encrypted at the edge, and why use it on top of SSL/TLS?

values.display: applications that have the private keys
edge locations can encrypt the credit card data

qualifiers.scope: CloudFront Field-Level Encryption, on top of SSL/TLS

evidence.quote: With field-level encryption, CloudFront’s edge locations can encrypt the credit card data.
From that point on, only applications that have the private keys can decrypt the sensitive fields.
This ensures a higher level of security since even if one of the application services leaks cipher text, the data remains cryptographically protected.

claim: Dedicated IP Custom SSL allocates dedicated IP addresses to serve your SSL content at each CloudFront edge location. Because IP addresses map one to one to SSL certificates, it works with browsers and other clients that do not support SNI.
question: Which CloudFront custom SSL option works with clients that do not support SNI?

values.display: clients that do not support SNI

qualifiers.scope: Dedicated IP Custom SSL, each CloudFront edge location

evidence.quote: Dedicated IP Custom SSL allocates dedicated IP addresses to serve your SSL content at each CloudFront edge location.
Because there is a one to one mapping between IP addresses and SSL certificates, Dedicated IP Custom SSL works with browsers and other clients that do not support SNI.

claim: SNI Custom SSL relies on the SNI extension of Transport Layer Security, which lets several domains serve SSL traffic over the same IP address. Older browsers that do not support SNI cannot connect to load the HTTPS version of your content. SNI Custom SSL costs nothing beyond standard CloudFront data transfer and request fees.
question: What does SNI Custom SSL rely on, which clients cannot use it, and what does it cost?

values.display: multiple domains to serve SSL traffic over the same IP address
Older browsers that do not support SNI cannot establish a connection
no additional cost beyond standard CloudFront data transfer and request fees

evidence.quote: SNI Custom SSL relies on the SNI extension of the Transport Layer Security protocol, which allows multiple domains to serve SSL traffic over the same IP address by including the hostname viewers are trying to connect to.
Older browsers that do not support SNI cannot establish a connection with CloudFront to load the HTTPS version of your content.
SNI Custom SSL is available at no additional cost beyond standard CloudFront data transfer and request fees.

note: FAQ item 89. Three small claims about one option; if the entail vote splits them, the adjudicator may split the fact.

claim: Dedicated IP Custom SSL is $600/month, prorated by the hour, because of the current IP address costs.
question: What does CloudFront Dedicated IP Custom SSL cost per month, according to the FAQ?

qualifiers.condition: prorated by the hour; price as stated in the FAQ

evidence.quote: Due to the current IP address costs, Dedicated IP Custom SSL is $600/month prorated by the hour.

note: FAQ item 89. The FAQ gives no per-what unit beyond '$600/month prorated by the hour'.

note: FAQ item 91. Link also acm-faq-cloudfront-us-east-1 (Region rule) from the ACM chapter.

evidence.quote: Note that CloudFront still supports using certificates that you obtained from a third-party certificate authority and uploaded to the IAM certificate store.

claim: CloudFront has an optional private content feature. When it is enabled, CloudFront delivers files only when you say it is okay by securely signing your requests.
question: Does CloudFront support access controls for paid or private content, and how do they work?

evidence.quote: Yes, Amazon CloudFront has an optional private content feature.
When this option is enabled, Amazon CloudFront will only deliver files when you say it is okay to do so by securely signing your requests.
